planting.note: Direct sow in fall into dry, gravelly, well-drained soil in full sun; Western Wallflower is a biennial-to-short-lived perennial that reseeds readily once established.

directions: Plant in full sun in dry, rocky or gravelly, well-drained soil; Western Wallflower bears spikes of orange-to-yellow flowers, sometimes tinged purple, from spring into early summer on a biennial-to-short-lived-perennial mustard reaching 12-24 inches. It grows naturally on dry plains, roadcuts, and foothill slopes across the shortgrass steppe into the Rocky Mountains, tolerating lean soil and drought once established. It reseeds reliably in congenial conditions, maintaining a population over time even though individual plants are short-lived.

planting.note: Direct sow in fall into dry, gravelly soil in full sun; White Locoweed is an ornamental planting only, not a livestock forage area, since it is toxic to grazing animals.

directions: Plant in full sun in dry, gravelly, well-drained soil; White Locoweed is a legume with silvery, silky-haired pinnate leaves and dense racemes of cream-white to pale-lilac pea flowers, blooming April through June on a low mound 6-12 inches tall. It is a classic shortgrass and mixed-grass prairie species on dry gravelly soil from the Great Plains into the Rocky Mountain foothills. Known as 'locoweed' for its toxicity to grazing livestock, it is safe as an ornamental planting but should not be sited where livestock might browse it.

planting.note: Direct sow in fall into dry, gravelly, well-drained soil in full sun; Easter Daisy blooms very early, often among the first high-plains wildflowers to open each spring.

directions: Plant in full sun in dry, gravelly or rocky, well-drained soil; Hooker's Townsendia is a nearly stemless, cushion-forming daisy relative with disproportionately large white-to-pink ray flowers and a yellow disc, blooming very early in spring, often March to April, among the first wildflowers to appear on the high plains. Its tiny, ground-hugging rosette fits well in a rock garden or shortgrass steppe planting where its outsized blooms provide a surprising early-season show. It needs sharp drainage and tolerates extreme drought once established.

planting.note: Direct sow in fall into dry prairie or clay/shale soil in full sun; Two-Grooved Milkvetch is a selenium-accumulating species and should not be planted where livestock might graze it.

directions: Plant in full sun in dry prairie, roadside, or clay/shale soil; Two-Grooved Milkvetch is an upright legume reaching 1-2 feet, bearing dense, spike-like racemes of pale purple-to-lavender pea flowers from May through July. It is common across the dry Great Plains shortgrass and mixed-grass zone, including shale and clay outcrops, and is one of several selenium-accumulating Astragalus species, meaning it should be sited away from livestock grazing areas. It is drought-tolerant once established, needing little water beyond its first season.

planting.note: Direct sow after last frost into dry, rocky or caliche soil in full sun; Hairy Tridens is a specialty-seed item with intermittent stock, so confirm current availability before planning a planting.

directions: Plant in full sun in dry, rocky or caliche soil; Hairy Tridens is a low, tufted warm-season bunchgrass reaching 6-12 inches, with fuzzy white-haired seedheads appearing in summer. It is characteristic of dry, rocky shortgrass plains and limestone outcrops, most pronounced toward the southern high plains of the Texas and Oklahoma panhandles. Availability through specialty native-seed sources can be intermittent, so confirm current stock before planning a planting, but it is a genuine, correctly documented native grass worth seeking out for a dry shortgrass steppe restoration.
